questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of the standard LCS dynamic program for strings of length m and n?
questions.explanation: It fills an (m+1)×(n+1) table with O(1) work per cell, giving O(mn) time and space.

questions.prompt: How does a subsequence differ from a substring?

options.text: A subsequence preserves order but need not be contiguous
A subsequence must be contiguous; a substring need not be

questions.explanation: A subsequence keeps relative order but may skip elements; a substring is a contiguous run. LCS and LIS are about subsequences.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Edit distance runs in O(mn) time
Longest increasing subsequence can be found in O(n log n)
LCS finds the longest contiguous common substring

questions.explanation: LCS and edit distance are O(mn); LIS has an O(n log n) method. LCS is about a (possibly non-contiguous) subsequence, not a substring.

questions.prompt: The minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions to turn one string into another is the ______ distance. (Levenshtein or the common one-word name)
questions.explanation: This is the edit (Levenshtein) distance, computed by an O(mn) DP.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to solve LCS with a bottom-up table.

items.text: Initialize the empty-prefix row and column to 0
Fill each cell from the recurrence

questions.explanation: Allocate the table, set the empty-prefix base cases, fill in dependency order, and read the bottom-right cell.

questions.prompt: Match each problem with its description or complexity.

pairs.right: Longest increasing subsequence, O(n²) or O(n log n)

questions.explanation: These sequence problems share a prefix-indexed DP shape; a subsequence is the order-preserving, gap-allowing selection they operate on.
